# Factorize

Hosted workflow: connect your agent → create a skill → run it → inspect the result → configure its trigger.

Application: https://app.factorize.sh
MCP (Streamable HTTP + OAuth): https://app.factorize.sh/mcp

Browser: unique username signup, username or email/password login, skill settings, execution/provider connections and consent.
MCP: discover targets, manage triggers, invoke with retained idempotency keys, inspect state/context/diagnostics.
Current MCP does not return execution output; inspect browser traces or REST trace pages. REST is not full MCP parity.

Generated from maintained guides in navigation order. Do not edit this file directly.

## Factorize with your agent
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/

Factorize hosts your trigger configuration, event routing, queue, run history, and MCP endpoint. Your external agent and hosted Pi use the same MCP tools and team skills. Pi runs inside Factorize with PostgreSQL persistence and an optional remote workspace.

Start at [app.factorize.sh](https://app.factorize.sh). Connect your agent to `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, create a manual trigger, inspect its result, then add a schedule or provider event.


  [Connect your agent](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview): Authorize a remote MCP client
  [First trigger](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart): Review a repository and inspect the result


Configure an OpenAI-compatible provider URL and optional key in Integrations,
then choose a model and permissions in Team settings. Add an exe.dev or Fly
workspace only when a task requires a VM. Each user receives a personal team;
skills, Triggers, runs and integrations live directly in that team.
[Self-hosting](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/deployment) is optional.

## Connect your agent
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview

Use the remote **Streamable HTTP** endpoint:

```text
https://app.factorize.sh/mcp
```

Complete [browser account and execution setup](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart) first. Factorize requires OAuth authorization, owner membership and tenant-bound scopes. A JSON configuration from one client is not a universal MCP configuration.

## Codex

Current Codex supports Streamable HTTP and OAuth. Add this client-specific TOML to `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.factorize]
url = "https://app.factorize.sh/mcp"
```

Run `codex mcp login factorize`, then use `/mcp` in Codex to verify the connection. See the [official Codex MCP documentation](https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp) for configuration and OAuth support.

## Claude Code

Add the remote server:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http factorize https://app.factorize.sh/mcp
```

Start Claude Code, enter `/mcp`, choose Factorize and authenticate when prompted. See the [official Claude Code MCP documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp) for HTTP transport, OAuth and configuration scope.

## Authorize in the browser

The client opens Factorize authorization in your browser. Sign in with your verified Factorize email/password and approve the requested scopes. Select `triggers:read` for discovery, `triggers:write` for edits, `runs:read` for inspection, `runs:invoke` for Trigger invocation, `runs:start` for direct runs, and `runs:cancel` for cancellation. Integration and skill operations use their respective scopes. Read-only access cannot create or invoke triggers. Return to your client after consent.

Consent lists 12 permissions, including `runs:write` for renaming runs. Run write grants also retain invocation and cancellation access for compatibility. Write does not imply read. If you need to create an account or verify your email, finish those steps and restart client authorization; do not assume the signup screen will automatically resume the original request. No Linear or execution token belongs in the MCP client.

Ask **“List my Factorize triggers.”** The agent should call `list_triggers({})`. An empty `items` list is a successful connection to a workspace with no triggers. Next ask it to list execution integrations and follow the [first-trigger walkthrough](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart).

Other clients must support remote Streamable HTTP and Factorize's OAuth discovery/PKCE flow. Their UI and plan availability vary; consult their own documentation rather than pasting either configuration above.

## Connection problems

For rejected consent, expired authorization, missing targets, scope errors and reconnection steps, see [connection troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/connection). Protocol implementers should use [authentication](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/authentication) and [discovery](https://docs.factorize.sh/api/discovery).

## Built-in workflow skills

Factorize publishes five build-shipped workflows through the [MCP Skills extension](https://skills.extensions.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/beta/skills), `io.modelcontextprotocol/skills`, on protocol revision 2026-07-28 or later:

- **manage-presets:** VM, permission and model presets and team defaults.
- **manage-skills:** live team-skill discovery, authoring, safe editing and dependencies.
- **run-and-supervise:** dispatch, completion subscriptions, results and intervention.
- **manage-triggers:** schedules, webhooks, lifecycle automation and delivery diagnostics.
- **manage-environments:** reflection, integrations, exe.dev/Fly.io VMs and renewable proxy grants.

A compatible client discovers the extension in `server/discover`, calls `skills/list`, inspects `skills/get`, and reads Markdown through `resources/read`. The complete catalog contains five entries with no further pages. Every operation requires an active authenticated identity; built-in instructions do not require `skills:read` or grant application/integration permissions.

Canonical `skills/WORKFLOW/SKILL.md` files in the repository are embedded into the build, with no runtime database or filesystem lookup. The same standard Markdown can later be packaged into a ChatGPT or Claude plugin; plugin packaging is not included here. `npm run generate:skills` regenerates the embedded catalog and `npm run check:skills` detects drift. Both Worker deployment scripts regenerate it before bundling. URIs have the form `skill://factorize/CONTENT_VERSION/WORKFLOW/SKILL.md`; content versions are derived from the complete catalog. Manifests contain exact SHA-256 digests and UTF-8 byte lengths. Content and URIs are identical across teams, scopes and runs, change only with a new build, and carry a one-hour private cache hint. After an upgrade, rediscover the catalog if an old version URI is rejected.

## Live team skills and pinned run inputs

Editable team skills are application data. Discover and read them with `list_skills` and `get_skill`, requiring `skills:read`; author them with the skill mutation tools and their write scopes. Team edits, renames and deletions never change the built-in catalog. Existing authorized `skill://teams/TEAM_ID/SKILL_NAME/...` resource reads remain supported for compatibility, but team packages are not returned by `skills/list` or `skills/get`.

Selected run skills are pinned inputs under `skill://runs/TEAM_ID/RUN_ID/SKILL_NAME/SKILL.md`, including supporting files. An active owning run may read supplied pinned resource URIs even without `skills:read`. Those inputs do not appear in extension discovery or `skills/get`. Unrelated edits, renames and deletes do not replace the run's accepted package. Broader team-library discovery still requires `skills:read`.

Factorize-managed Pi uses this same MCP boundary. Its short-lived identity is bound to the active run and current execution lease. Application scopes and selected integrations come from the accepted run snapshot. Cancellation, lease replacement, owner revocation and integration disconnection are checked on subsequent requests. Provider credentials never enter model context.

Completion notifications require a client/host adapter that supports `subscriptions/listen`, reconnects and reads the returned outcome URI. Without that support, use `get_run` while active or explicitly check the run later; installing a workflow skill does not add background notification delivery to a client.

## Proxy tool discovery

Integration APIs are available through `request_api`, without a VM, shell, or raw
OAuth credential. Call `get_api_reflection` first and pass an integration's
`requestExample` to `request_api`. Use `read_api_response` for retained handles.
The proxy tools remain discoverable when `proxy:use` has not been granted; calls
then fail with `insufficient_scope` and require renewed consent. `forbidden`
indicates integration policy; `credential_unavailable` asks the owner to repair
upstream credentials.

If reflection is available but proxy tools are missing, compare authenticated
server `tools/list` with the connector's catalog. From a repository checkout,
pipe the captured JSON into `node scripts/diagnose-mcp-proxy.mjs`. This diagnostic
makes no network calls. If server discovery includes the missing tools, refresh
or reconnect the client connector; otherwise check the deployed server version.
A saved connector catalog can differ from the current repository. Local fixture
acceptance verifies the protocol contract, not a particular mobile app release.

## Your first skill
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart

## Set up in the browser

1. Sign up at [app.factorize.sh/auth/signup](https://app.factorize.sh/auth/signup),
   choose a unique username, verify your email and sign in. Your personal team uses your username. You can sign in with your username or email, plus your password.
2. In **Integrations**, add a model integration with an
   OpenAI-compatible provider URL and optional access key. In **Team settings**,
   open **VM** and choose that integration and a provider model ID. Configure run permissions under **Permissions**.
3. For repository or shell work, connect an exe.dev or Fly account and enable
   **Requires VM** in the Team defaults. exe.dev tokens need ls, new, ssh and rm.
   The guest needs a workspace shell; it does not need Pi, Codex, Claude or model
   credentials. Pi runs in Factorize and uses MCP to reach that workspace.
4. [Connect your MCP client](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview), approve the workflow scopes and ask
   it to call get_team and get_api_reflection. Integration grants are separate
   from application scopes. Select provider credentials in Permissions.

A VM preset copies workspace settings into a Trigger's **VM** section or Team
run defaults. Editing the preset does not change accepted runs or existing
saved configurations.

## Create and run a skill

Open **Skills**, choose **New skill**, and save its name and instructions. Overview includes instructions, a read-only directory browser, and **Start run**. The skill's **Runs** tab includes manual and event-triggered runs.

Under **Settings**, use **General** for execution mode and prompt, **VM** for workspace/model/concurrency defaults, **Permissions** for access, and **Trigger** for event sources and enable/disable controls. A trigger is optional and can include multiple event sources. Manage the library's Git repository under **Team Settings → Skills**.

**Account settings → Profile** changes your unique username and personal team name together.

## Existing MCP trigger clients

Existing REST/MCP trigger tools remain compatible. For example:


Ask your agent:

> Inspect my team defaults and permissions. Create a manual Trigger named
> review-recent-changes. Have it reflect on the environment, clone
> https://github.com/YOUR_ORG/YOUR_REPO.git in its required workspace, review the
> latest commit, run relevant checks and summarize the results. Invoke it once
> with a stable idempotency key and report the observed result.

Expected tools:

1. get_team: inspect the saved defaults. Do not invent integration IDs.
2. list_triggers: check for an existing Trigger before creating one.
3. create_trigger: supply the definition below and save its returned id.
4. invoke_trigger: use that ID and a stable idempotencyKey; save runId.
5. get_run: poll for state, failure diagnostics and trigger_result. Open its
   browser trace when more execution output is needed.

```json
{
  "name": "review-recent-changes",
  "requiresVm": true,
  "prompt": "Reflect on the environment. Clone https://github.com/YOUR_ORG/YOUR_REPO.git into the workspace. Review the latest commit, run relevant checks, and summarize problems.",
  "concurrencyLimit": 1,
  "events": [{"kind": "manual", "config": {}}]
}
```

```json
{"triggerId":"TRIGGER_ID","prompt":"Review now","idempotencyKey":"review-recent-changes-first-run"}
```

The Trigger must return an id and manual Event with a stable generated slug.
Invocation returns runId promptly. Submission alone is not completion: inspect
get_run until terminal and assess the actual result. A selected unavailable VM
or model integration is an error; Factorize does not silently switch providers.

After a timeout, repeat the invocation with the same key to recover its original
receipt. A failed run still owns that key. Inspect external effects before
starting a new run. After a successful manual review, add a
[schedule](https://docs.factorize.sh/recipes/scheduled-review) or [provider Event](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events).

## Skills and presets
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/skills

The team navigation contains **Skills**, **Runs**, **Integrations**, and **Settings**. Skills appear in a table with name, description and a **Run** action. Run launches that skill directly and opens its run. Preset choices and trigger settings remain on the skill detail page. Global search matches only skill names and run names.

## Skill definition

`SKILL.md` is the source of truth. The editor provides frontmatter controls and plain text editing of the Markdown body. Unrelated frontmatter is preserved. Overview renders the body as Markdown and retains the directory browser.

```yaml
---
name: review-pr
description: Review a pull request
metadata:
  factorize:
    vm-preset: development
    permission-preset: repository-write
    model-preset: careful
    concurrency: 0
    disabled: false
---
Review the pull request and report findings.
```

Preset references are human-readable slugs, unique within preset type and team. Omit a preset key to inherit that type's team default. Overview selectors update and commit these same fields immediately. Inside the editor, all controls and the body save together in one conditional revision. A stale save fails without overwriting another edit; reload before reapplying it.

`concurrency` is a nonnegative integer and defaults to **0**, meaning unlimited simultaneous runs of that skill. Team capacity still bounds total running work. `disabled` defaults to false. Disabled skills cannot start new manual or automated runs; existing accepted runs continue. Script-based run creation is retired. A skill can use its agent tools to execute code.

## Team presets

**Team Settings → VM**, **Permissions**, and **Models** each contain a preset list. Add and Edit open dedicated pages. The action menu also selects a team default or deletes a preset after confirmation. Each type has one team default. Default presets cannot be deleted; select another default first. Skills referencing a preset block deletion until those references are changed. Display names can change; slugs stay fixed.

VM presets select a provider, connection, image, and provider-specific size/region or tags, or explicitly select no VM. Permission presets select application scopes, integration access and permitted invocation destinations. Model presets select a model account/provider, model and effort. Team capacity remains editable under VM.

Presets are references. Every edit creates an immutable preset revision. When a run is created, before queueing, Factorize freezes the resolved configuration, each preset's ID/slug/revision, whether it was inherited, and the skill commit. Editing a preset or switching team defaults affects future runs. Accepted runs retain their original configuration and skill files.

## Automation and files

Each skill has **Overview**, **Runs**, and **Triggers** tabs. Triggers configures only automatic event sources. Manual events are hidden legacy details; manual runs remain available from Runs and API/MCP. Old skill Settings links redirect to Overview or Triggers.

The directory browser displays nested text files and identifies binary files. Supporting files remain intact when instructions are edited. Published content is cached by tenant, repository and immutable commit. Manage repository selection and sync under **Team Settings → Skills**.

## Clone and edit with Git

Open **Skills → Code → HTTPS** to copy the authoritative repository URL. The **Skill settings** link opens repository selection and sync settings.

For Factorize-managed skills, the URL is `https://git.factorize.sh/<team-name>/skills.git`. Repository names stay stable when a team is renamed; teams with the same name receive a numeric suffix. Select **Get Git token**, then use username `git` and the token as your Git password. Tokens last one hour and are limited to that repository and your current team membership. Password changes or membership revocation invalidate existing tokens. Keep tokens in your Git credential manager, outside the clone URL.

```bash
git clone https://git.factorize.sh/my-team/skills.git
cd skills
# Edit skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md and supporting files.
git add .
git commit -m "Update skill instructions"
git push origin main
```

Pushes to `main` publish through the same validation and synchronization used by Factorize's Git push workflow. Skill files and preset references must be valid before they appear in the library. A rejected synchronization retains the previously published library and reports the repository error in Skill settings.

For GitHub-sourced skills, the menu shows `https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>.git` and the tracked branch and folder. Authenticate directly to GitHub using your own GitHub CLI, credential manager, or personal access token. Factorize never exposes its GitHub App token. Push changes to GitHub; Factorize's internal mirror is read-only and syncs from the configured GitHub source.

## Migration and API clients

Existing distinct configurations become presets, with equivalent configurations reused. Existing extra saved prompts are preserved in the Markdown body. Legacy script automation is disabled; historical runs remain readable. Migration can resume after a failed file publication without duplicating presets or instructions.

REST clients use `/api/v1/presets` for listing/creation, `/api/v1/presets/{id}` for updates/deletion, and `/api/v1/presets/{id}/default` to select defaults. Preset updates accept `expectedRevision`; omitting it preserves last-writer-wins compatibility. Skill writes accept a complete `body` or structured `definition`, with `expectedRevision` on updates. Changing a skill’s execution metadata also requires `triggers:write`. Legacy team run-default writes update the corresponding default preset revisions; capacity-only writes leave presets unchanged. The former skill execution-settings write returns `settings_retired`; update frontmatter or presets instead.

MCP exposes `list_presets`, `create_preset`, `update_preset`, `set_default_preset`, `delete_preset`, `get_skill`, `create_skill`, `update_skill`, `get_skill_trigger` and `save_skill_trigger`. Direct `start_run` may select `vmPreset`, `permissionPreset` and `modelPreset` slugs for that run. Direct-run permissions remain bounded by the caller's effective access.

## Create and edit triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/triggers

In the browser, open a [skill](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/skills), then **Triggers**. Each skill has at most one optional trigger, which can contain several event sources. Execution configuration belongs to SKILL.md and its referenced presets, and the browser uses its name to label the trigger.

The following describes the compatible REST/MCP trigger interface. Existing trigger IDs, names and write omission semantics remain available to external clients.

Ask: “List execution integrations and triggers, then create a review trigger for this repository.” Use [the first-trigger input](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart) and [MCP tool contract](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools). Reuse an existing trigger when its name/purpose matches; trigger creation has no idempotency key.

`update_trigger` **replaces configuration**, rather than patching one field. Always call `get_trigger` first. Build a write object containing `triggerId`, `name`, `prompt`, `requiresVm`, optional `executionConfigId`, `runNameTemplate`, `concurrencyLimit`, `model`, optional `effort`, and the full intended `events` array. Preserve each existing event's `id`, `slug`, `kind`, `enabled`, and writable `config`. Strip read-only response fields (`triggerId` inside events, timestamps, reflection, secretConfigured and destination). Do not pass the entire read response unchanged.

Triggers using exe.dev may set optional `vmImage` to a public Docker/OCI image reference such as `ghcr.io/org/image:tag`. Leaving it blank uses exe.dev's default image. In the trigger editor, **Verify image** creates a temporary owned VM, checks SSH and workspace prerequisites, and deletes the VM; it never runs the trigger prompt. Verification is explicit and autosaving does not create VMs. Private images and registry credentials are not supported. Verification records what worked at that time; mutable tags may later resolve to a different image.

Supply `expectedUpdatedAt` from the fetched trigger's `updatedAt` to protect against concurrent edits. On `stale_trigger`, fetch again and reapply the desired changes. Omitting it retains last-writer-wins behavior. Omitted optional configuration resets to defaults; omitted events remove the configured automatic events. Preserve all events you want to keep.

After saving, call `get_trigger` and compare prompt, target and events. `enable_trigger` and `disable_trigger` change enabled state without rebuilding configuration. Disabling automation does not stop an existing run. Trigger saves can event `edited` lifecycle subscribers. Deleting a Trigger removes its template and events. Runs and artifacts follow their normal retention period.

## Names

The browser displays the owning skill name and has no separate trigger-name field or skill selector. Skill renames preserve IDs and run history. The compatibility API still accepts a trigger's internal name in its existing shared resource namespace; use the name returned by `get_trigger` when updating through that interface.

## Team and skill defaults

Skills select VM, permission and model presets through SKILL.md frontmatter. Missing selections inherit the corresponding team default. Preset configurations are resolved and frozen before a run queues. Configure only automation on the skill Triggers page; legacy manual events are hidden. See [Skills and presets](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/skills) for metadata, concurrency, disabled behavior and migration.

## Write Trigger context
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/prompts

An agent Trigger has one optional skill and one optional prompt. The skill body and prompt remain literal, including any Mustache-looking text. Put repository, task, validation, and reporting instructions in either.

Each Event has an optional Mustache `template`. Only the firing Event's template contributes text. A missing or blank template contributes nothing, regardless of payload size. Use selected fields for salient details, for example `Issue {{issue.identifier}}: {{issue.title}}`. `{{webhook}}` explicitly inserts the full normalized webhook Event object. It is never included automatically.

Agent input is composed in this order: skill instructions, Trigger prompt, rendered Event text, and manual caller instructions. Empty sections are omitted. A skill-only run is valid. An agent invocation with no skill or effective instructions fails before a run is queued or a VM is provisioned. Script-based run creation is retired. Skill instructions come from the Markdown body of SKILL.md; its frontmatter controls execution configuration.

Inside an Event template, fields are available directly. Manual Events have `prompt` and `data`; scheduled Events have `occurredAt`, `externalId`, and `metadata.timezone`; provider Events include prepared delivery fields such as Linear `issue` and ClickUp `task`. Terminal lifecycle Events have `sourceTriggerId`, `sourceRunId`, `state`, `completedAt`, and `outputs`. Edited Events have `source_trigger_id`, `event`, and `edited_at`. Idle Events have `source_trigger_id`, `event`, and `completed_at`.

Run-name templates retain access to structured Event data even when that Event has no prompt template. Returned Event slugs form stable namespaces, for example `{{event-2.issue.title}}`. Use the actual returned slug. Event namespaces take precedence over identically named payload fields. Full raw fields remain available through `{{webhook}}` for webhook Events.

Missing/null scalar paths become empty text. Objects and arrays interpolate as compact JSON with sorted object keys and preserved array order. Double braces preserve URLs, quotes, Markdown, and code as plain text. Sections and array iteration use the original structured values.

In Context settings, select an Event and open **Preview run context**. Supply a sample Event data object and optional manual instructions. REST `POST /api/v1/triggers/preview` and MCP `preview_trigger_prompt` use the same renderer. Preview includes the effective prompt and run name without saving or executing.

The cutover preserves old prompt ciphertext and skill links. Existing global templates are copied into Events. Triggers that previously selected multiple skills are paused until one explicit context choice is saved. Historical accepted skill snapshots and run prompts remain readable.

## Inspect results
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/results

Ask: “Show the latest runs for this trigger and summarize the completed review.” Use `list_runs({"triggerId":"JOB_ID","limit":10})`, then `get_run({"runId":"RUN_ID"})`. Current MCP does not return an `output` field or trace messages. Open the browser run page to read the trace, or retrieve REST trace pages with an authorized client. Report the state/link through MCP and only summarize findings after actually reading them.

Run pages return `items` and `nextCursor`; send that cursor for the next page. Optional `state` and `contextQuery` filter runs. Context search is a case-insensitive substring, not a query language. Current list rows contain no context excerpt; `get_run` returns full `context`, rendered `prompt`, `invocation.event_id`, execution metadata and activity.

Check that the intended event fired, the repository/task appears in the rendered prompt, and the browser/REST trace supports the reported result. A queued submission is not a successful execution. Browser run pages are at `https://app.factorize.sh/runs/RUN_ID`. Agent output stays in Factorize and is not automatically copied into Linear.

New agent runs must write a JSON result envelope to the absolute path in `FACTORIZE_RESULT_PATH` before exiting. The object requires `status` (`succeeded` or `failed`); it may include a `summary` and an `outputs` JSON object. Failed results require a non-empty `reason`. The file is limited to 64 KiB. A zero process exit without a valid `succeeded` result is a failed run. Put additional run files in `~/.factorize-trigger/`; regular files up to 10 MiB each (100 files, 50 MiB total) are retained. Symlinks and paths outside that directory are not collected. Run details show the result and authorized downloads.

For missing output or execution failures, call `get_run_diagnostics` and follow [failed-run troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/runs).

Failed runs keep the existing `failed` state filter and legacy `failure_source` enum (`system` or `agent`); `agent` maps to the canonical `failure.source: "run"`. New read responses include nullable `failure: { source: "run" | "system", code, reason }`. A null value means the historical evidence is unknown, not that the row was successful. Old rows that only have `failure_source="system"` are not treated as confirmed infrastructure failures.

Classification is based on execution evidence, never text in agent-controlled JSON. A failed structured result, missing/invalid required result, or unsuccessful agent process exit is a run failure. Launch/provisioning failure, unavailable run-owned VM, or disappeared supervisor is a system failure. A successful process and successful result has no failure. A successful result cannot override an unsuccessful process or an accepted `report_run_error`; when multiple task reasons disagree the first persisted execution/result failure is primary and explicit report provenance remains in `agent_error`. Independent infrastructure evidence takes system precedence. Result protocol failures are recorded as the failure reason, not as `artifact_error`. `artifact_error` remains reserved for artifact, trace projection and cleanup diagnostics.

Protocol version 0 runs keep optional-result compatibility. Protocol version 1 requires a valid result envelope (strict fields, maximum 64 KiB); malformed, oversized, missing or schema-invalid files fail the run. The result and report-error schemas do not accept a failure source or infrastructure provenance.

Historical repair is evidence based. Migration `0032_run_failure_outcomes.sql` only repairs failed rows with `trigger_result.status="failed"`, a successful execution diagnostic, systemd `Result=success`, and exit status 0. It clears `artifact_error` only when it exactly equals the structured task reason. Before rollout, run this read-only audit and retain its counts with a database snapshot:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS proven_run_failures,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE artifact_error=trigger_result->>'reason') AS exact_misplaced_artifact_reasons,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE artifact_error IS NOT NULL AND artifact_error IS DISTINCT FROM trigger_result->>'reason') AS retained_artifact_diagnostics
FROM app.runs
WHERE state='failed' AND failure_source='system'
  AND trigger_result->>'status'='failed'
  AND execution_diagnostics->>'state'='succeeded'
  AND execution_diagnostics->'systemd'->>'result'='success'
  AND execution_diagnostics->'systemd'->>'execMainStatus'='0'
  AND coalesce(trigger_result->>'reason','') <> '';
```

Roll forward with the additive migration before serving the new UI/API. Roll back application code separately and leave repaired outcome data intact; the old API ignores the new columns. Do not reverse the repair by changing every `agent` source back to `system`; unknown historical rows remain unknown.

## Background runs

Select team VM, permission and model defaults through the preset API or Team Settings. Team capacity uses `PUT /api/v1/team/run-defaults`. Script-based run creation is retired. Skill frontmatter references presets; missing selections inherit team defaults. Direct launches require the separate `runs:start` scope. A verified parent run can launch within its team, bounded by its own permissions. Run execution defaults belong to the team. Finishing the parent leaves the child running.

Call `start_run` with a literal prompt, optional skill key or ID, and a client-generated idempotency key. Supply `projectId` when an external client has multiple projects. Retrying the same request returns the same run. A launch skill is captured by ID, key and revision. Filter `list_runs` by `skillId`, using `none` for unclassified runs.

Save the receipt's `outcomeUri` with the originating conversation ID. With MCP revision 2026-07-28, request `subscriptions/listen` with that URI in `notifications.resourceSubscriptions`. On acknowledgment and on each resource update, call `resources/read`. A terminal outcome has a stable `eventId`, state, available result, failure and artifact references. Append it to the originating conversation once per event ID. Reopen the listen stream on close or reconnect. Older clients can read the resource directly. Reading or watching requires `runs:read`. Outcomes share the run's history retention period.

## Run telemetry and estimated costs

Hosted Pi records OpenTelemetry/OpenInference run, turn, model, tool, retry and
compaction spans without requiring Phoenix. Open a run's **Info** tab for live
wall time, usage and estimated cost. Expand a span for its timings and paged
input/output. Credentials and temporary file URLs are redacted; capture follows
run retention. Historical runs without capture remain readable.

Input totals include cache reads/writes; reasoning is already included in output.
Unreported usage and unknown model prices display as unavailable. Estimates use
an exact model-name match from a versioned Phoenix catalog snapshot. In
**Integrations → Edit model integration → Estimated model prices**, add USD rates
per million tokens for custom models or negotiated pricing. Each completed model
call saves its applied rates; later changes do not rewrite historical estimates.

The repository's `node scripts/update-model-prices.mjs` refreshes the bundled
catalog from Arize Phoenix. Pass a local manifest file to validate/update without
network access. Catalog provenance and generation date are exposed through the
model-pricing API. Updating the catalog is a reviewed source change; normal runs
and validation do not depend on live price downloads.

## Phoenix Cloud export

Configure the team in **Integrations → Phoenix Cloud telemetry** with the Phoenix
base URL (including `/s/YOUR_SPACE` for Phoenix Cloud), project name and API key.
Use **Test Phoenix connection** to verify access. Enabling exports captures new
runs automatically; it does not backfill older runs. The key is encrypted and
never returned to the browser. Omit it when editing to retain the configured key.

Completed spans enter a durable queue and are sent in bounded OTLP protobuf
batches. Transient errors retry with backoff, up to eight attempts; permanent
errors remain visible. Delivery is at least once: an ambiguous acknowledgement
can cause the same trace/span IDs to be sent again. Local capture and run results
remain available during an outage. Disable or disconnect to cancel pending
exports; neither action removes telemetry already received by Phoenix.

Run Info shows pending/sent/failed/canceled counts, export errors, and **View in
Phoenix** once the destination project ID is known. Link lookup retries separately
from ingestion, preserving successful delivery without retransmitting spans.
Large captured inputs/outputs use bounded previews with local content references.

## Stop and retry runs
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/stop-retry

Ask: “Inspect this run, stop it if it is still active, and verify its final state.” Fetch `get_run`, then use `stop_run({"runId":"RUN_ID"})` for a starting, running or blocked run. The response requests `stopping`; poll until terminal and inspect diagnostics for cleanup.

**Current behavior:** `kill_run` calls the same stop operation as `stop_run`. Stopping a queued or reserved run records a terminal stopped outcome before VM launch. Both return `operation_failed` when the run is not active. Do not treat kill as stronger recovery; contact the hosted operator if a run remains stuck.

For a timed-out manual submission, repeat `invoke_trigger` with the **same** `idempotencyKey`. The response contains the original `invocationId`, `runId`, and `duplicate: true`. Retain the key you submitted: current `get_run` does not return `invocation.idempotency_key`. Never send its internal `invocation.claim_key` or a `manual:` prefix back as the key. If the key was lost, inspect existing runs before requesting another.

To report a problem without stopping the agent, call `report_run_error` (or `POST /api/v1/runs/{runId}/report-error`) with a reason, continue any useful remaining work, and then exit normally. The first reason is retained: identical retries are safe, while a different replacement reason returns a conflict. Terminal runs reject reports. A report never changes polling, evidence collection, cleanup, or slot accounting.

An intentional new run after failure needs a new key. First verify that the prior run is terminal, inspect whether it made external changes, and fix the cause. A retry may repeat those external effects: invocation deduplication is not transactional rollback of the agent's work. For `queue_full`, wait for capacity and reuse the key for the intended request. See [failed runs](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/runs).

## Schedule a repository review
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/recipes/scheduled-review

User request:

> Review the latest commit in https://github.com/YOUR_ORG/YOUR_REPO.git every weekday at 09:00 UTC. Keep a manual event and report findings in Factorize.

First complete a [manual run](https://docs.factorize.sh/quickstart). Fetch the trigger, preserve its writable configuration and manual event identity, and append:

```json
{"kind":"schedule","enabled":true,"config":{"cron":"0 9 * * 1-5","timezone":"UTC"}}
```

Save with `update_trigger` and `expectedUpdatedAt`. Fetch again to discover the schedule's stable slug. Use a repository review prompt that works without manual context; optionally set the schedule Event template to `Scheduled at {{occurredAt}}`. Preserve the entire Event list when saving.

Expected result: an enabled weekday schedule and one queued/executing run at the next matching occurrence (subject to queue coalescing). Verify cron/timezone and next occurrence in the browser editor, then `list_runs({"triggerId":"JOB_ID"})` and `get_run`: the invocation's event ID and context must match the schedule, and the browser trace output must contain the review. Do not claim automation verified until a scheduled occurrence has actually run.

## Run a trigger from Linear
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/recipes/linear-trigger

User request:

> When an issue in my selected Linear project moves to my selected Ready status, run the repository agent to investigate it and report the result.

In browser [Integrations](https://app.factorize.sh/integrations), connect Linear, approve workspace access, and select an accessible project/status in the trigger editor. The execution account separately needs repository and Linear access if the prompt asks it to read/update Linear. MCP does not list Linear projects/statuses or connect accounts; use browser resource selection to obtain the IDs.

Create a trigger with the required [trigger fields](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools), repository instructions, and this event (replace both IDs):

```json
{"kind":"webhook","enabled":true,"config":{"provider":"linear","projectId":"PROJECT_ID","matchRules":[{"type":"status","targetId":"STATUS_ID"}]}}
```

Factorize adds the manual event. Fetch the saved trigger to obtain the webhook slug/reflection. Safely replace configuration with an Event template such as `Clone REPOSITORY_URL. Investigate this Linear issue: {{event-2.issue.title}}. Issue context: {{event-2}}. Run relevant checks and report evidence.` Use the actual webhook slug, preserving all other configuration.

Expected result: a matching issue change delivers an event and starts a run; all configured rules must match. Move one test issue into the selected status. Verify `list_webhook_deliveries({"provider":"linear","triggerId":"JOB_ID"})`, inspect the delivery timeline and `list_trigger_webhook_activity`, then check the run's firing event, issue context, then inspect output in the browser trace. Factorize does not automatically post execution output to Linear. For absent/rejected events follow [triggers not firing](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events).

## Automate from GitHub
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/github

[Connect the Factorize GitHub App](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/oauth) in the browser and approve the selected repositories. Ask `list_github_installations({})` for safe installation IDs. Select the repository in the browser trigger editor to obtain its numeric repository ID; MCP does not provide a repository picker.

Append this event to a successful manual trigger, preserving the complete configuration:

```json
{"kind":"webhook","config":{"provider":"github","installationId":12345,"repositoryId":67890,"event":"pull_request","action":"opened"}}
```

Replace illustrative IDs with the selected installation/repository IDs. GitHub requires either non-empty issue match rules or both event and action. Read the saved event's slug/reflection before using fields such as `{{event-2.pull_request.number}}`. Give the execution agent its own repository access.

Open one test PR on the selected repository. Verify delivery timeline, trigger activity and run context, then output in the browser trace. Missing events often mean wrong repository selection, a suspended installation or event/action mismatch. Use [event troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events). Delayed conflict workflows also verify live PR state; conditions previews do not perform that verification.

## Automate from ClickUp
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/clickup

[Connect ClickUp](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/oauth) in Integrations and approve access to the intended team/list. Factorize registers the task webhook on connection. Use the browser trigger editor to select a list and rule target IDs; MCP does not discover ClickUp lists/statuses.

Add this event to the complete trigger configuration:

```json
{"kind":"webhook","config":{"provider":"clickup","listId":"LIST_ID","matchRules":[{"type":"status","targetId":"STATUS_ID"}]}}
```

Replace IDs with browser-selected values. All configured rules must match. Read the returned stable slug/reflection before using `{{event-2.task}}` in the prompt. Ensure the execution agent separately has any ClickUp access required to work on the task.

Change one test task to the selected status. Verify delivery with `list_webhook_deliveries({"provider":"clickup"})`, inspect its timeline, trigger activity and resulting run. Reconnect in Integrations if provider authorization expires; use [event troubleshooting](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events) for rejected or absent deliveries.

## Chain triggers
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/recipes/chaining

User request:

> After my review trigger succeeds, run a second trigger to inspect its findings. Keep the follow-up manually runnable.

Discover source trigger ID with `list_triggers`, and choose a target with `list_execution_configs`. Create the destination with required trigger fields and:

```json
{"kind":"triggerLifecycle","enabled":true,"config":{"sourceTriggerIds":["SOURCE_JOB_ID"],"states":["succeeded"]}}
```

Read the destination's returned event slug, then preserve all writable fields/events while setting that Event's template to `Inspect source trigger {{event-2.sourceTriggerId}} and run {{event-2.sourceRunId}}. Summarize its findings.` Use the actual slug. Context includes identifiers, `state`, `completedAt`, and structured `outputs`. Include outputs explicitly through the Event template when needed. The execution agent must have its own authorized way to retrieve source results (for example its own Factorize MCP access); the conversational client's authorization is not forwarded. If unavailable, have the conversational agent inspect the source output in the browser or via REST trace pages and manually invoke the destination with output in `data` instead of claiming automatic output transfer.

Expected result: a successful source run produces a destination run. Invoke the source with a stable key, wait for success, then inspect destination runs and full context to verify source trigger/run IDs, then inspect output in the browser. Avoid cycles and make prompts safe for repeated events; automatic signals may coalesce.

Available states are `succeeded`, `failed`, `stopped`, and `edited`. **Edited** fires on successful saves (including enable/disable), even unchanged saves, not creation or run-state changes. Edited context has `source_trigger_id`, `event: "edited"`, and `edited_at`; it has no source run ID. Only same-tenant enabled subscribers match, and a trigger cannot subscribe to its own edits. Pending edit events wait while disabled/unmatched; deleting the source or removing the event discards them. Verify an edited recipe by saving the source and inspecting the destination context.

## Manual trigger invocation permissions
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/work/manual-invocation-permissions

For preset-backed skills, configure allowed destination triggers in a **permission preset**. Every accepted run captures those destinations, bounded by its caller or parent run. Later preset edits affect future runs. Direct and automated runs use the same captured grants; disabling a skill prevents new runs without modifying accepted ones.

The legacy standalone trigger API can read destinations with `GET /api/v1/triggers/{triggerId}/invocation-permissions` and replace them using `PUT` with `{"destinationTriggerIds":["..."]}`. Destinations must belong to the same team. For a skill-backed trigger, reads expose effective preset destinations and writes return `permissions_retired`; update the permission preset instead. Run credentials cannot edit invocation permissions. [Skills and presets](https://docs.factorize.sh/work/skills) describes defaults and run snapshots.

## Connect your accounts
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/oauth

Factorize accounts own dashboard identity. Sign up with an email and password, verify your email to sign in automatically, then open [Integrations](https://app.factorize.sh/integrations) to connect Linear when using Linear-backed triggers. Linear OAuth only connects the workspace; it never signs you in. Register `/auth/linear/callback`, configure issue and issue-label webhooks at `/webhooks/linear`, and store the client credentials and signing secret as Worker secrets. ClickUp is optional: register `/auth/clickup/callback`; connecting it automatically registers its task webhook. GitHub uses an installed GitHub App, while exe.dev and Cloudflare Tail connections are configured in Integrations.

| Account | Browser action and required access | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| exe.dev | Add an account-level token, test credentials, and save. VM configurations select workspace images and tags; managed agents use hosted Pi with a separate model integration. Needs VM listing/creation/SSH/deletion, per-run WIF integration management and exclusive VM attachment; see [operations](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/operations). | Test connection, then `list_execution_configs`; optionally diagnose the saved connection. |
| Linear | Connect Linear and approve the workspace. Your account must access the selected project and issues; organization policies may require an administrator. | Select project/rules in the browser editor, send one matching event, inspect delivery/run. |
| ClickUp | Connect ClickUp and approve the intended workspace/team with access to the list/tasks. | Select list/rules, change one matching task and inspect delivery/run. |
| GitHub | Connect GitHub to install/authorize the Factorize App on the intended account/repositories; organization approval may be required. | Confirm active installation and repository selection, then send a matching event. |

The provider consent/installation screen is the authority for granted permissions. Grant access to the selected resources; changing those resources can require provider reauthorization. Trigger-event access and execution-agent access are separate: select an existing GitHub installation or Linear connection in each trigger to authorize its backend proxy access. Factorize reuses those credentials and their existing upstream permissions; it does not deliver tokens to the VM.

MCP exposes safe connection/installation/target metadata, not tokens. Account connections, resource pickers and credential management require browser setup. Reconnect Linear/ClickUp from Integrations; use GitHub's Configure installation link for repository access and verify the installation is active. Do not disconnect integrations while triggers still reference them; update those triggers first.

After changing access, create one controlled event and use `list_webhook_deliveries`, `get_webhook_delivery`, `list_trigger_webhook_activity`, and `list_runs` to verify delivery and execution. See [triggers not firing](https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events). Hosted Factorize manages OAuth application registration, callbacks and webhook infrastructure. Operators of their own deployment use [configuration](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/configuration).


## Credentials selected by a trigger

In Integrations, add custom bearer credentials with a fixed HTTPS
origin. Add model integrations with an OpenAI-compatible provider URL and an optional API key. Factorize encrypts credentials on the server. Stored secrets cannot be viewed. A keyless provider requires only its URL. Model IDs and optional effort are selected in Team defaults, Triggers, or direct run overrides, independently of VM configuration.

Select only the bearer integrations, GitHub installations, Linear connection and model integration that each Trigger needs. Pi runs in Factorize and uses MCP tools. Skills can use their VM tools to execute code.
Each run uses its saved selection and Factorize API scope snapshot; later trigger
edits affect future runs. Disconnect revokes existing run access permanently,
even after reconnecting the same account. Select a replacement explicitly for
future runs. Missing selections remain visible for repair and are never
silently replaced with all available credentials.

exe.dev and Fly guests use a localhost helper that authenticates to Factorize
with fresh vendor signatures bound to that exact VM/run. Selected upstream
credentials stay in the backend. Canceling or terminating a run removes its API
and outbound access, independently of external VM deletion retries.

## MCP API proxy access

External MCP clients continue to authenticate with OAuth; execution VMs continue
to use vendor OIDC. These identities have separate grants. Run selections never
inherit an external client's approvals.

In Integrations → MCP API access, choose a policy for each custom
bearer integration, GitHub installation, Linear connection, and model account:

* **Baseline:** immediately available to all active MCP authorizations. Removing
  baseline access immediately removes access derived from that policy.
* **Requestable:** visible in reflection, but each separately authorized
  connection must obtain consent before use.
* **Disabled:** unavailable for requests and consent. Disabling or disconnecting
  permanently invalidates existing integration approvals. Re-enabling as
  requestable requires fresh consent. Replacing a credential without deleting
  its integration preserves approvals.

Start OAuth with only the Factorize resource scopes your client needs; do not
request the complete integration catalog. `get_api_reflection` returns the
current agent identity, effective Factorize scopes, integration references,
readable names and descriptions, instructions, access state, connection
availability, and the required integration scope. Availability describes stored
connection state, not a guarantee that an upstream credential is healthy.

POST JSON to the reflected `proxy.requestUrl` with `integration`, an HTTP `method`, a relative `path` including
an optional query, optional safe `headers`, and optional `body`. `encoding` is
`utf8` by default or `base64` for binary input. The origin and upstream
credentials are selected by Factorize. A grant covers the whole integration,
bounded by the credential's upstream permissions. Redirects are rejected.

Missing requestable access produces an HTTP 403 response with a
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge containing `error="insufficient_scope"`,
`scope`, and `resource_metadata`. Reauthorize with the union of your currently
needed scopes and the challenged scope, approve the named integration in the
browser, exchange the new code, then retry. The new authorization is independent
of other connections, including copies of the same client. Refresh retains the
authorization identity; a narrowed token uses only its presented scopes.
Integration scopes have the form `integration:{reference UUID}:{revocation epoch}`;
use the value returned by reflection rather than constructing or caching it.

Responses preserve the upstream `status`, safe `headers`, byte `size`, and body.
An upstream non-2xx status is distinct from a local authorization or proxy error.
UTF-8 responses of up to 32 KiB return inline with `encoding: "utf8"`; binary
responses use `base64`. Larger responses are consumed into R2 and return a
`handle` and `expiresAt`.

POST JSON to `proxy.readResponseUrl` with the handle and a byte `offset` (initially zero).
Chunks are always base64, up to 64 KiB; use `nextOffset` until `done` is true.
Handles are tenant/identity bound, expire after 30 minutes, and recheck access on
every read. Revocation blocks subsequent calls and reads but cannot undo an
upstream action already accepted. Existing VM proxy URLs retain true streaming.

The same operations are documented under `/api/v1/agent/reflection`,
`/api/v1/agent/requests`, and `/api/v1/agent/responses/read`. Authorize `proxy:use` to use the HTTP proxy with the agent credential. Existing MCP authorizations without this scope require renewed consent. Other REST operations retain their own authentication requirements. MCP clients use `request_api` and `read_api_response` with the same validated arguments and authorization as these HTTP endpoints. Owner policy endpoints require an interactive browser session. In **Settings → Authorized clients**, choose **Edit permissions** to disable or restore originally authorized Factorize scopes. For each integration, choose **Default** to follow workspace policy and OAuth consent, **Allow** to approve the current integration, or **Block** to deny this connection access. Disabling or disconnecting a workspace integration invalidates per-connection approvals. Edits apply to subsequent requests from this connection and its delegated VMs. Owners can also revoke a connection. MCP clients can set their own connection label with `rename_mcp_client`.

The scheduler maintenance heartbeat removes expired response objects and their
PostgreSQL receipts. A receipt exists before any R2 block is written, including
interrupted/unreturned responses. Object deletion failures retain receipts for
retry. Operators must retain the scheduler and RUN_ARTIFACTS binding when
rolling out migration `0054_agent_api_grants`.

## External VM access

Start Codex with the device login helper from the Factorize checkout:

```sh
node scripts/agent-login.mjs codex
```

Approve the displayed code. The helper sets the short-lived Factorize credential for the child process and configures the Factorize MCP connection to use it. Supply additional integration scopes from reflection in the space-separated `FACTORIZE_SCOPES` environment variable on a subsequent login. In a shell with this environment, send JSON to the reflected request URL using `curl -H "@$FACTORIZE_AGENT_AUTH_FILE" --json ...`. The file is private to your OS user and the helper removes it when the child exits. For exe.dev, send method `POST`, path `/exec`, headers `{"Content-Type":"text/plain"}` and a command in `body`.

After creating a VM, call `grant_vm` with the reflected provider integration ID, VM name (exe.dev) or Machine ID (Fly.io), selected integration IDs and an idempotency key. Fly.io also requires the app name. Reflection advertises the eligible provider as `vmGrantProvider`. The guest obtains its provider OIDC token and local proof using the receipt instructions; those authenticate only the HTTP proxy operations. Provider credentials and the parent client token never enter the VM.

New grants last one hour. Call `renew_vm_grant` before expiry to reset the timeout to one hour from renewal. Renewal requires the same active OAuth authorization and continuing access to the provider and all selected integrations. A refreshed client token can explicitly renew; client token refresh alone, proxy requests and creation retries do not extend a grant. Expired/revoked grants require a new grant with a new idempotency key. Parent authorization revocation and integration access removal/disconnection block subsequent access. Existing grants retain their stored expiry until explicitly renewed.

For exe.dev, the guest reads its dedicated WIF token endpoint. For Fly.io, it requests a fresh JWT by POSTing the receipt audience to the local OIDC endpoint through `/.fly/api`. OIDC token renewal proves current VM identity; it does not renew the one-hour Factorize grant. Follow the returned proof-file and proxy URL instructions for either provider. Access through independent provider-native integrations is outside this grant. Revocation removes the exe.dev Factorize identity integration; Fly has no per-grant provider attachment. Both leave the VM running.

## Event configuration
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events

Schedule config is `{cron, timezone}`. Webhook config supports `linear` (`projectId`, non-empty `matchRules`), `clickup` (`listId`, rules), `github` (`installationId`, `repositoryId`, and rules or event/action), and `cloudflareTail` (`integrationId`). Match rule types are `owner`, `creator`, `status`, `label`, and `assignee`, each with a `targetId`.

Lifecycle config is `{sourceTriggerIds, states}`, where states are `succeeded`, `failed`, `stopped`, or `edited`. Events have stable server-generated slugs (`event-1`, `event-2`, …); use them in Mustache templates. Disabled events do not fire.

Terminal lifecycle events (`succeeded`, `failed`, and `stopped`) are recorded transactionally when a watched run changes into that state. Creating a subscription, enabling a disabled subscription, re-enabling it, or changing its watched triggers or states starts matching from subsequent terminal transitions; existing terminal runs are not replayed. A run already in progress when a subscription starts is delivered if it reaches a watched terminal state afterward. Prompt and other unrelated trigger edits do not move this boundary. Events captured for an enabled subscription remain pending while its destination is disabled, and are delivered after it is enabled again; removing the event or deleting the source run discards its pending event. Delivery retries are deduplicated by event and source run state.

For hosted triggers, connect the provider in [Integrations](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/oauth), select accessible resources in the browser editor, and verify a matching event with delivery tools. Factorize verifies provider signatures and manages OAuth subscriptions. Optional Cloudflare Tail events require your own source/relay integration; infrastructure setup belongs in [operations](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/operations).

Choose **Trigger lifecycle → Edited** and one or more source triggers to run a trigger when another trigger is saved (including enable/disable saves). Creation and run status changes do not produce edit events. Each successful save is an event, even if the submitted values are unchanged. Only enabled subscribers in the same tenant are matched; a trigger cannot subscribe to its own edits.

Edited events expose `{{event-1.source_trigger_id}}`, `{{event-1.event}}` (`edited`), and `{{event-1.edited_at}}`. Events are recorded in the save transaction and delivered by the scheduler with retry deduplication. Subscribers added later do not receive earlier edits. Pending events wait while the destination is disabled or no longer matches; removing a event or deleting its source trigger discards them.


Webhook event configuration accepts optional `conditions`, a json-rules-engine
condition tree, not a full rule/engine configuration. No conditions means no
additional filtering. `all`, `any`, and `not` compose leaf conditions; empty groups
are invalid. Invalid configuration or evaluation failures never create a run.
Provider authentication, scope/event/action selection and matchRules still apply.

```json
{"all":[{"fact":"webhook","path":"$.check_suite.conclusion","operator":"equal","value":"success"},{"fact":"webhook","path":"$.check_suite.head_branch","operator":"startsWith","value":"feature/"}]}
```

`webhook` is the only fact. It contains the prepared context the trigger receives:
original provider fields, provider/event/delivery_id metadata, and existing
Linear `issue`/ClickUp `task` aliases. Tail context has already been sanitized.
Delayed GitHub dequeue verification still checks an open PR targeting main,
retries unresolved mergeability, and only proceeds on confirmed conflict. Its
prepared pull_request includes verified mergeable=false and mergeable_state.
Conditions use the latest event configuration and never transform context.

JSONPath supports `$`, ordinary `.property` and quoted bracket properties,
array indexes `[0]`, and wildcards `[*]`/`.*`. No recursive descent, slices,
unions, filters, scripts or executable expressions are accepted; expression
evaluation is disabled. A scalar path returns its selected value (including an
array when selecting an array field). A wildcard path always returns an array
of matches, even for zero or one match. Missing scalar paths yield undefined.
`notEqual` may match missing fields; null and missing are distinct. Malformed
paths are configuration errors, not non-matches.

| Operator | Configured value | Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| equal / notEqual | string, number, boolean or null | Strict scalar equality/inequality; string IDs differ from numeric IDs |
| lessThan / lessThanInclusive / greaterThan / greaterThanInclusive | finite number | Both operands must be finite numbers; strings/null/missing do not match |
| in / notIn | array of scalar values | Strict membership/non-membership of the selected value in the configured array |
| contains / doesNotContain | scalar | Strict array membership/non-membership; a non-array selected value does not match |
| startsWith | string | String prefix; missing/null/non-string selected values do not match |

Boolean negation follows the library semantics: `not` negates a valid result,
including a non-match due to a wrong operand type. No existence operator is
introduced. Conditions are limited to 16,384 serialized UTF-8 bytes, depth 16
(root counts as 1), 128 nodes, and 512 characters per path. User priorities,
fact references in values, callbacks and network facts are rejected.

The editor provides conditions JSON and prepared-example JSON textareas.
POST `/api/v1/trigger-conditions/test` and MCP `test_trigger_webhook_conditions` accept
`{conditions?, webhook}` with triggers:write authorization. The context is limited
to 262,144 serialized bytes; the HTTP request is limited to 300,000 bytes.
They return `decision: match | no-match | error` plus plain JSON result details.
Configuration/request validation errors return a validation error. Details with
no `result` were not evaluated, and must not be displayed as failed. The preview
does not authenticate the example, route events, verify live GitHub state, or
invoke triggers. Runtime activity stores only concise decisions, never these values.

## Connection problems
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/connection

| Symptom | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Browser consent fails or is cancelled | Sign in to the correct verified Factorize owner account, restart authorization from the client, and approve the requested scopes. Finish signup/email verification separately before restarting. |
| Client never connects | Confirm the exact URL `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp`, remote Streamable HTTP and OAuth support. Open the client's MCP status view and authenticate; use [client-specific instructions](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview). |
| `invalid_token` or access disappears | Reauthorize the client. Password resets/changes and sign-out invalidate delegated credentials. An expired access token needs client refresh or renewed login. |
| `insufficient_scope` | Reconnect and grant `triggers:read` for discovery, `triggers:write` for Trigger edits, `runs:read` for inspection, `runs:write` for renaming, `runs:invoke` for invocation, and `runs:cancel` for stop. |
| `list_execution_configs` returns no items | In dashboard Integrations, test and save an exe.dev or Amp integration in the same workspace. MCP cannot create credential-bearing connections. |
| Target exists but repository/model access fails | Test the saved execution integration and check execution-account repository/model access and VM tags. For exe.dev, `diagnose_exe_integration` uses the saved connection ID and creates/deletes a temporary VM. |

To reconnect access, open [Account settings → Authorized clients](https://app.factorize.sh/settings/authorized-clients), revoke the old client if necessary, remove/reconnect its authorization in the MCP client, then authorize again. Verify with “List my Factorize triggers” followed by “List my execution integrations.” Revocation affects access, not stored triggers. Provider reconnection is separate: use [Integrations](https://app.factorize.sh/integrations).

## Triggers not firing
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/events

1. Fetch `get_trigger`; confirm the trigger and intended event are enabled. Check schedule timezone/cron, selected provider resources, and all matching rules.
2. Make one controlled matching provider event. Ask for `list_webhook_deliveries` filtered by `provider` and `triggerId`; if nothing is found, search by provider alone since unmatched deliveries may not link the trigger.
3. Use the returned delivery's identifier with `get_webhook_delivery` to inspect its safe timeline. Use `list_trigger_webhook_activity` for matching, rejected, duplicate and accepted activity. No raw payloads or secrets are returned.
4. If no delivery appears, reconnect the provider in Integrations, check resource access/app installation and provider delivery status. Ask the hosted operator to investigate transport/subscription failures; hosted users do not configure Factorize's webhook signing secrets.
5. If delivery appears but no run does, check event/action selection, match rules and conditions. `test_trigger_webhook_conditions` previews prepared example context only; it does not authenticate or deliver an event.
6. Check `list_runs`: automatic occurrences coalesce while a run is queued. An accepted run may be waiting for an active slot. Query the provider itself for authoritative work.

For schedules, verify the next occurrence in the browser editor, timezone and enabled state, then inspect runs after that time. For lifecycle events, verify source IDs/state selection and same-tenant source triggers. A destination cannot subscribe to its own edits. See [event configuration](https://docs.factorize.sh/integrations/events).

## Failed or stuck runs
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/troubleshooting/runs

Ask:

> Investigate run RUN_ID. Show its prompt and lifecycle diagnostics, and link to its browser trace for output. Identify the failure and whether it changed anything externally. Do not create a duplicate run; recommend a safe recovery.

Call `get_run({"runId":"RUN_ID"})` then `get_run_diagnostics({"runId":"RUN_ID"})`. Expected evidence includes `state`, `execution`, `trace`, `artifact`, `harnessLog` and `activity`. Check launch, prompt delivery, output capture, claim release and cleanup rather than treating a missing trace as proof the agent never ran.

| Evidence | Recovery |
| --- | --- |
| `failure.source` is `run` | The agent/script could not complete, including required result protocol errors and process exits. Read the primary failure reason, result and trace. |
| `failure.source` is `system` | Positive launch, VM or supervisor evidence prevented execution or supervision. Use execution diagnostics and contact the operator if it persists. |
| Failed with `failure: null` | Historical failure evidence is unknown. Do not infer system failure from legacy `failure_source` alone. |
| Queued | Inspect active runs/concurrency with `get_trigger`; wait for a slot. |
| Launch or permission failure | Check the model integration URL/key and provider model. If Requires VM is enabled, check the selected workspace connection, image and tags. Use `list_exe_connections` then `diagnose_exe_integration({"connectionId":"CONNECTION_ID"})` if appropriate. Image verification uses a disposable VM. |
| Wrong/empty prompt values | Read actual event slug/reflection and persisted context; safely replace the full trigger configuration. |
| Failed with useful output | Fix the reported cause, inspect the browser trace and check external changes, then request a new manual run with a new idempotency key. |
| Starting/running/blocked but stuck | Request `stop_run`, poll, and inspect cleanup. `kill_run` stops execution immediately and cleans up asynchronously. Escalate persistently stuck runs to the hosted operator with run ID and safe diagnostics. |
| Missing/partial trace | Inspect output and artifact state; ask the owner/operator about REST-only retained-artifact replay. See [advanced operations](https://docs.factorize.sh/self-hosting/operations). |

Worked recovery configuration: use the original trigger ID and `invoke_trigger({"triggerId":"JOB_ID","prompt":"Retry after correcting repository access","idempotencyKey":"investigation-RUN_ID-retry-1"})` only after fixing the cause and confirming the old run is terminal. Expected result is a **new** run ID. Verify its rendered prompt/state with `get_run` and successful output in the browser trace; a diagnostic probe passing does not itself prove the trigger succeeds. Artifact and cleanup diagnostics are separate from the primary failure and never change an already resolved outcome.

## MCP tool reference
Source: https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/tools

Connect to `https://app.factorize.sh/mcp` using [client authorization](https://docs.factorize.sh/mcp/overview). Tools return text containing JSON and the same JSON in `structuredContent`. Array service results are wrapped as `{"items":[...]}`; object results retain their fields. Examples below show structured content, sometimes with selected fields only. Identifiers such as `JOB_ID` are placeholders: use returned identifiers, never invented values.

## Inventory

The inventory below lists the scope required by each tool. Scopes are explicit. `runs:write` authorizes run renaming and error reports.

| Tool | Required scope | Input contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list_exe_connections` | integrations:read | `{}` |
| `list_github_installations` | integrations:read | `{}` |
| `diagnose_exe_integration` | integrations:write | Required string `connectionId`; credential-safe diagnostic |
| `list_cloudflare_tail_integrations` | integrations:read | `{}` |
| `list_triggers` | triggers:read | `{}` |
| `get_trigger` | triggers:read | Required string `triggerId` |
| `create_trigger` | triggers:write | Required `name`; optional skill, prompt and Event templates; execution settings inherit Team defaults |
| `update_trigger` | triggers:write | Same required trigger fields plus `triggerId`; optional `expectedUpdatedAt` and `runScopes` |
| `delete_trigger` | triggers:write | Required string `triggerId`; deletion retires the template and events |
| `enable_trigger` | triggers:write | Required string `triggerId` |
| `disable_trigger` | triggers:write | Required string `triggerId` |
| `get_team` | team:read | `{}`. Returns the authenticated team and its shared run defaults. |
| `list_runs` | runs:read | Optional `triggerId`, `state`, `contextQuery`, `limit`, `cursor` |
| `get_run` | runs:read | Required string `runId` |
| `rename_run` | runs:write | Required `runId` and `name`; optional `expectedName` |
| `get_run_diagnostics` | runs:read | Required string `runId` |
| `report_run_error` | runs:write | Required `runId` and `reason`; records an error without stopping execution |
| `list_presets` | integrations:read | List all team preset types, immutable slugs/revisions, and defaults. |
| `create_preset` | integrations:write | `kind`, immutable `slug`, display `name`, and type-specific `settings`. Permission presets also require triggers:write. |
| `update_preset` | integrations:write | `presetId` and `preset` with the same fields plus optional `expectedRevision`. Creates a new revision. |
| `set_default_preset` | team:write | `presetId`; affects future inherited runs. |
| `delete_preset` | integrations:write | `presetId`; defaults and referenced presets are protected. |
| `get_skill_trigger` | skills:read, triggers:read | `skillId`; returns automatic events only. |
| `save_skill_trigger` | skills:write, triggers:write | `skillId` and `trigger` containing events, enabled and optional expectedUpdatedAt. |
| `start_run` | runs:start | Optional literal `prompt` and one optional `skill` (at least one effective input), `inputs`, `requiresVm`, `executionConfigId`, `modelAccountId`, `name` and `idempotencyKey`. Optional `vmPreset`, `permissionPreset` and `modelPreset` select preset slugs. Script-based run creation is retired. Returns `runId`, the browser `url`, `outcomeUri`, and `duplicate`. |
| `invoke_trigger` | runs:invoke | Required string `triggerId`; optional `name`, `prompt`, `data`, `idempotencyKey` |
| `rename_mcp_client` | Authenticated OAuth connection | `{ "name": "Release assistant" }`. Sets this connection’s display name in Settings → Authorized clients. Names are trimmed and accept 1–120 characters. |
| `get_api_reflection` | Authenticated OAuth/run identity | `{}`. Discover the authorization identity, effective scopes, and granted/requestable integration APIs, including instructions, required OAuth scope, and connection availability. |
| `fetch_media` | Selected integration and active run, or runs:start plus proxy access | Capture unchanged image bytes from an integration-relative GET path; returns an artifactId for read_media. |
| `read_media` | Own active run input/scratch, or own upload with runs:read | Read original image content from an artifactId using standard MCP image blocks. |
| `vm_exec` | Active hosted run with a bound workspace | Execute `command` and optional absolute `cwd` in the verified current VM; returns output and exitCode. No arbitrary VM selector. |
| `create_payload` | proxy:use for OAuth; active run identity | Reserve a temporary file body and authenticated browser upload link; optional name, mediaType and byteSize |
| `append_payload_chunk` | Originating connection/run | Required handle, byte offset and bounded body; optional utf8/base64 encoding |
| `finalize_payload` | Originating connection/run | Required handle; optional SHA-256; finalizes immutable bytes |
| `import_attachment` | proxy:use for OAuth; active run identity | Native OpenAI file object with download_url, file_id and optional mime_type/file_name |
| `fetch_payload` | Selected authorized integration | Integration ID and relative path; optional name/mediaType; imports exact bytes |
| `get_api_operation` | Originating authorized proxy identity | Required operationId; polls durable state without repeating the HTTP request |
| `read_api_operation` | Originating authorized proxy identity | Required operationId; optional offset/limit; bounded incremental base64 bytes |
| `cancel_api_operation` | Originating authorized proxy identity | Required operationId; cancellation cannot undo upstream writes |
| `query_api_response` | Same access as the original request | Retained handle; mode json/text/bytes, bounded expression/offset/limit/maxResultBytes |
| `request_api` | proxy:use for OAuth; selected integration for runs | Credential-injected HTTP request with integration, method, relative path, optional headers/body and encoding |
| `read_api_response` | Same identity and integration grant | Read a retained response handle at an optional byte offset |
| `grant_vm` | vm:grant and proxy:use | Delegate explicit integration IDs for one hour to an exe.dev VM or Fly.io Machine. Requires providerIntegrationId, vm, integrationIds and idempotencyKey; Fly.io also requires app. |
| `renew_vm_grant` | vm:grant and proxy:use | Required grantId; same parent OAuth authorization renews a live grant for one hour after rechecking provider and selected integration access. |
| `revoke_vm_grant` | vm:grant | Requires grantId. Invalidates guest access and schedules provider-specific cleanup; leaves the VM running. |
| `get_runtime_context` | Authenticated identity | `{}`; verified authentication kind, effective scopes, and source run/trigger IDs, without credentials |
| `get_trigger_invocation_permissions` | triggers:read | Required string `triggerId` |
| `set_trigger_invocation_permissions` | triggers:write | Required `triggerId` and `destinationTriggerIds` UUID array; owner session, scoped API key, or authorized OAuth client |
| `stop_run` | runs:cancel | Required string `runId` |
| `kill_run` | runs:cancel | Required string `runId`; currently the same stop operation |
| `list_trigger_webhook_activity` | runs:read | Required `triggerId`; optional integer `limit` (1–100, default 50) |
| `list_webhook_deliveries` | runs:read | Optional strings `provider`, `deliveryId`, `event`, `action`, `outcome`, `triggerId`, `q`, `from`, `to`, `cursor`; integer `limit` (1–100, default 50) |
| `get_webhook_delivery` | runs:read | Required string `deliveryId` |
| `test_trigger_webhook_conditions` | triggers:write | Required prepared JSON object `webhook`; optional `conditions` tree |
| `list_skills` | skills:read | Optional `q`, `limit`, and `cursor` |
| `get_skill` | skills:read | Required string `skillId` |
| `create_skill` | skills:write | Required `key` and `body` |
| `update_skill` | skills:write | Required `skillId` and `expectedRevision`; optional `key` and `body` |
| `delete_skill` | skills:write | Required `skillId` and `expectedRevision` |
| `list_skill_triggers` | skills:read | Required string `skillId` |
| `preview_trigger_prompt` | skills:read | Optional `skillId`, literal `prompt`, `eventTemplate`, `eventKind`, `eventSlug`, `eventData`, manual `instructions`, and `runNameTemplate` |

The inventory is validated against every registered implementation tool. All required IDs are non-empty strings except numeric GitHub installation/repository IDs in event configuration.

## Discovery inputs and outputs

- get_team exposes Team defaults. Select optional workspace configurations in the browser; model integration and model selection are independent of VM configuration.
- `list_exe_connections({})` returns safe connection IDs and available tags, never API tokens, guest agents or model catalogs.
- `list_github_installations({})` → `{"items":[{"installationId":12345,"accountLogin":"YOUR_ORG","state":"active"}]}` (selected fields). Use numeric `installationId` in GitHub events; choose repository IDs in the browser.
- `list_cloudflare_tail_integrations({})` → `{"items":[{"integrationId":"INTEGRATION_ID","name":"Worker errors","referencedTriggerCount":0}]}` (selected fields). Use `integrationId` in Tail event configuration.
